verses.1: Al-Mizan interprets al-burūj as the visible, elevated stations of heavenly bodies, comparable to prominent towers, rather than the twelve signs of the zodiac. The oath is by the heaven protected through these constellations, as in (15:16-17), and accords with the warning and glad tidings that follow.
verses.2: Al-Mizan identifies the Promised Day as the Day of Resurrection, when God has promised to judge among His servants.
verses.3: Al-Mizan takes the oaths in (85:1-3) together as four oaths supporting the sūrah's threat to persecutors of believers and its promise to the righteous. The protected heaven signifies that God will ward off the plots of devils and disbelievers; the Promised Day ensures recompense; and the Witness observes the persecution while the Witnessed is publicly seen. It reads shahādah in both shāhid and mashhūd as presence and observation, not courtroom testimony, though observation may lead to testimony before God; the absence of ʿalā supports this reading. The Witness can therefore be the Prophet, who observes his community and will testify, as in (33:45) and (22:78). The Witnessed may be the believers' persecution, its retribution, or the Resurrection's punishments and rewards; the indefinite forms magnify both. The commentary rejects the many proposed identifications when they assume testimony or use shahādah inconsistently. An editor notes that hereafter usage can mean testimony, but that the author gives the sūrah's theme and immediate context priority. The omitted answer to the oaths is inferred from (85:5) and (85:10-11): God threatens persecutors and promises steadfast believers protection from their schemes.
verses.4: Al-Mizan treats qutila as an imprecation—driving the People of the Ditch from God’s mercy—not as the complement of the preceding oaths. Al-ukhdūd means a trench or pit: the people were oppressors who made fiery ditches and burned believers for their faith, preparing the warning of (85:10). It rejects the view that they were the victims and qutila simply means ‘were killed’: the pronouns in (85:6), (85:7), and (85:8), especially their witnessing what they did and their vindictiveness, can only refer to the persecutors.
verses.5: Al-Mizan explains that the fire is an apposition to the Ditch and that al-waqūd is fuel; its abundance marks the fire's great size, intensity, and heat. The oppressors sat around it and watched the believers being consumed.

verses.8: Al-Mizan reads naqam as intense dislike: the persecutors hated the believers solely for faith in God. The Ever-Mighty, Ever-Praiseworthy, universal King, and Witness of all establish that the believers' faith was right, their persecution unjust, and God knows their suffering, will reward them, and will requite their oppressors. His might is invincible; His praise-worthiness means His acts are just and beautiful, encompassing jalāl and jamāl; His kingdom entails absolute command, judgment, lordship, and exclusive worship; and nothing of creatures or their deeds is hidden from Him. The commentary rejects the claim that the idolaters merely opposed denial of lesser gods while believing in God: they credited Him only with initial creation, but assigned rubūbiyyah—the universe's direction and management—and ulūhiyyah—the right to be worshipped—to idols, treating God only as Lord of lords and Deity of deities.

verses.10: Al-Mizan defines fitnah here as torture, trouble, and distress, and extends the persecutors beyond the People of the Ditch to Quraysh's torture of believing men and women to make them abandon faith. It reports Majmaʿ al-bayān's explanation that the punishment of hell and the punishment of burning are distinct: their torment is not confined to fire but includes other pains, such as Zaqqūm, ghislīn, and clubs.
verses.11: Al-Mizan presents the promised gardens and running streams as glad tidings that console believers, answering the preceding severe warning to those who persecute and torture them.
verses.12: Al-Mizan explains baṭsh as forceful, fierce seizure. The following verses confirm the earlier warning and glad tidings, while ‘your Lord’ consoles the Prophet with support and victory by assuring him that the oppressors among his own people will also meet this punishment.
verses.13: Al-Mizan reads ibdāʾ, contrasted with iʿādah, as origination, synonymous here with badʾ; it notes the rare reading yabdaʾu. God alone brings anything into being without assistance and restores whatever has expired, proving unrestricted power and explaining the severity of His seizure. No transient being can escape Him: He can impose a punishment beyond a transgressor's capacity, maintain it, and restore what punishment destroys so suffering continues, as in (35:36) and (4:56). The exclusive wording assigns both origination and return to God alone. He also sets the limits of things, including death as this world's limit of pain, and may remove or change such a limit in the hereafter. No one can deflect His command; only one divine command may qualify or take precedence over another.
verses.14: Al-Mizan understands the Ever-Forgiving and Ever-Loving as God's abundant forgiveness and love, corresponding to His promise of good to believers just as His severe seizure corresponds to His warning to disbelievers.
verses.15: Al-Mizan takes al-ʿarsh, a king's throne, metaphorically as God's sovereignty: He is the King with absolute authority to rule His kingdom as He wills. Al-Majīd denotes spiritual greatness and magnificence, hence perfection in essence and attributes.
verses.16: Al-Mizan says that no internal obstacle—boredom, sloth, exhaustion, or a change of mind—nor any external obstacle can impede God's will and decree. Together with His sovereignty and glory in (85:15), this proves His right and power to threaten persecutors with hell and promise paradise to believers; as Doer of what He wills, He does not break His promise.
verses.17: Al-Mizan says the stories of Pharaoh's and Thamūd's hosts reiterate God's severe seizure and His character as the Ever-Glorious King and Doer of what He wills. Their reference also consoles the Prophet.

verses.19: Al-Mizan apparently identifies the faithless with disbelievers from the Prophet's tribe. Bal signals that prior admonitions and arguments are ineffective because they persist in denial. Warāʾihim means the encompassing outer dimensions around them, so they cannot defeat or outmaneuver God, which consoles the Prophet. It records the alternative that warāʾ means ‘behind,’ alluding to their turning their backs on God.

verses.21: Al-Mizan reads bal as correcting the deniers: the Qur'an is not what they allege, but a recited book magnificent in meaning and filled with divine teachings. Its preserved tablet is kept from falsehood, untruth, and the reach of devils.
